newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says not causing strain in Greece relations.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says not causing strain in Greece relations.

text.p: Turkey said on Wednesday it was not to blame for any strain in relations with neighbouring Greece after Britain voiced concern about the possibility of war breaking out between the two NATO allies over Cyprus.
"If there is tension in Turkish-Greek relations, this is not caused by Turkey's attitude," Turkish foreign ministry spokesman Omer Akbel told a news conference.
"The Greek Cypriot side, with the full support of Greece, prefers the way of conflict instead of compromise," he said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcom Rifkind, speaking on BBC radio on Tuesday, said Athens and Ankara lacked the political will to find a solution.
"When relations are already bad and tense and difficult and both sides appear to be looking for an excuse to make them worse, that is pretty grim," he said.
Rifkind said he considered a conflict in the Aegean Sea between Turkey and Greece to be "a serious possibility".
Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides, on a visit to India, dismissed Rifkind's warning. Greece said Rifkind's comments were unjust and blamed Ankara for the tension.
Akbel said Turkey remained committed to solving problems with Greece through "peaceful methods".
Relations between Ankara and Athens have worsened in the last year as a dispute over territorial claims in the Aegean added to tensions.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in 1974 after a coup by the military then ruling Greece. Around 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed on the island.

Britain and the United States expressed alarm last month at a Greek Cypriot decision to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles, saying acquisition of the S-300 system could destabilise what is already one of the most heavily militarised areas of the world.
The decision to buy the weapons, due to be deployed next year, drew threats of a military strike from Turkey.
